S008.title: The folding number press

chapters.title: Count the choices on the press

transcript: This little printing press has one stamp in each place. Print a one in the hundreds, tens and ones. The strip reads one hundred and eleven. A number made entirely of ones is called a repunit. If each stamp prints three instead, what number will appear?

Three hundreds, three tens and three ones make three hundred and thirty three. Now fit four stamps. Fold the strip between its middle places. The ends meet, and the two inside places meet. Give each touching pair the same digit. Open the strip. It reads the same forwards and backwards. That is a palindrome.

Print two on the outside pair and seven on the inside pair. The result is two thousand seven hundred and seventy two. Can you divide it by eleven without long division? Lift the inside stamps. The outside pair contributes two thousand and two. Put the inside pair on a separate strip. Its value is seven hundred and seventy.

One thousand and one is eleven times ninety one. The outside pair therefore contributes eleven times one hundred and eighty two. One hundred and ten is eleven times ten. The inside pair therefore contributes eleven times seventy. Add the two quotients. One hundred and eighty two plus seventy is two hundred and fifty two.

Change the outside digit. Its two places still contribute that digit times one thousand and one. Change the inside digit. Its two places still contribute that digit times one hundred and ten. Both contributions are multiples of eleven, whatever digits you choose. Here is a harder order for the press. How many four digit palindromes are multiples of thirty three?

Thirty three is three times eleven. We already have the eleven. For the three, check the digit sum. Each chosen digit appears twice, so the digit sum is twice the sum of our two choices. Doubling cycles the remainders one and two into each other. Only zero stays zero. The two chosen digits must therefore add to a multiple of three.

Sort the inside digits by remainder. Zero, three, six and nine go in the first tray. The other trays have three digits each. Outside digits one, four and seven need the remainder two tray. That gives nine strips. Two, five and eight need the remainder one tray. Nine more. Three, six and nine need the first tray. That gives twelve. The order is filled with thirty different palindromes.

Could zero be an outside digit as well? Try printing zero, six, six, zero. The leading zero disappears. Six hundred and sixty has only three digits. Keep zero in the inside tray, though. Nine thousand and nine is a valid strip. Next time, pair the matching places, test the remaining condition, and count just the digits your press lets you choose.
S008.bridge: When the printing press shows 2,772, pause before the strip splits. How much of the number comes from the two outside 2s together? How much comes from the two inside 7s?

S137.title: Digit detectives
transcript: A train ticket reads seventy three. Turn its two digit cards around and it reads thirty seven. The same two digits are still here. Why did the value change by thirty six?
The seven loses nine groups of itself when it moves from tens to ones. The three gains nine groups of itself on the return trip. The net loss is nine times four, which is thirty six.
Here is another ticket. Its digits add to eleven. Its number exceeds its reverse by twenty seven. Before trying numbers, what do those clues tell you about the two digits?

Twenty seven is nine times three, so the tens digit is three larger. Set those three aside from the total of eleven. The remaining eight splits equally. The digits are seven and four. Seventy four minus forty seven really is twenty seven.
A three digit code exceeds its reverse by three hundred and ninety six. The middle digit is twice the last digit. All three digits add to sixteen. Which code opens the lock?

The middle digit stays in the tens column. Subtracting cancels it. Each unit of difference between the outside digits changes the number by ninety nine. Three hundred and ninety six is four groups of ninety nine. The first digit is four larger than the last.

Call the last digit one part. The middle takes two parts. The first takes one part and four extra. Remove four from sixteen. Four equal parts share twelve, so the last digit is three. The code is seven, six, three.

Seven hundred and sixty three minus three hundred and sixty seven is three hundred and ninety six. The middle digit cancels in the subtraction, but still counts in the digit sum. In a new digit puzzle, track which positions change and which clues still use every digit.
S137.bridge: Watch what each digit gains or loses when it moves one place. In the lock, look for the digit that stays put.

S138.title: Read the flow bench

chapters.title: Read the rise and the run
Draw the trace without a leak

transcript: On this flow bench, one meter counts water arriving. A second meter counts water escaping. A pen records how much water remains. The difference between the two rates tells us how quickly the pen rises or falls.

Seven litres enter each minute and two litres leave. Pair two outgoing marks with two incoming marks. Five litres stay each minute. Starting empty, how much collects in three minutes? Three groups of five give fifteen litres.
Now nine litres enter each minute, but the leak meter is covered. The pen reads ten litres at minute one and thirty four litres at minute five. Both flow rates are steady. How fast is water escaping?

From ten to thirty four is a rise of twenty four litres. From minute one to minute five is four minutes. Six litres stay each minute. Nine enter, so three litres per minute escape. Six litres per minute for four minutes accounts for the whole rise.

Start a ten minute test with eight litres. The inlet delivers seven litres per minute throughout. The leak starts open, losing two litres each minute, then closes. The final reading is sixty six litres. At which minute did the leak close?

Imagine the leak were closed from the start. Eight litres plus seventy would give seventy eight litres. The actual finish is twelve litres lower. Each open minute accounts for two missing litres. Twelve divided by two gives six open minutes.

Check the bend at minute six. While the leak is open, six minutes at five litres per minute add thirty litres. The reading is now thirty eight. In the last four minutes, seven litres per minute add twenty eight more. Thirty eight plus twenty eight gives sixty six.

One trap is to keep subtracting the leak after the valve shuts. Mark each valve change and find the net rate for each interval. If the inlet and outlet rates are equal, the trace is flat, even while both meters turn.
S138.bridge: Follow the pen until the valve closes. What changes at the bend, and which flow keeps its old rate?

S141.title: Where the bars begin
transcript: These creek readings look dramatic. One blue bar seems twice as tall as the other. Before deciding that the water is twice as deep, read the number at the bottom of the scale.

The axis starts at thirty centimetres. The water was thirty six centimetres deep on Monday and forty two on Tuesday. The rise is six centimetres. Restoring the missing thirty shows why twice the visible height is only seven sixths of the original depth.

Two tanks are shown on a second chart. The bottom line means twelve litres. Every interval adds two litres. One bar rises three intervals and the other rises seven. What is the ratio of the fuller tank to the other?

Three intervals add six litres, so the smaller tank contains eighteen. Seven intervals add fourteen litres, so the larger one contains twenty six. Twenty six to eighteen simplifies to thirteen to nine. Seven to three compares the visible pieces alone.

The bottom label has rubbed off a chart. The values at the tops are thirty six and forty eight. The longer bar looks exactly three times as tall as the shorter bar. What number was on the bottom line?

Imagine sliding the short bar beside the long one. Their tops are twelve units apart. That gap is two short bars, because the long bar contains three of them. Each short bar therefore represents six units.
The shorter bar ends at thirty six. Step down six and the erased label must be thirty. Check the long bar. Forty eight minus thirty gives eighteen, which is exactly three times six.

Cropping the same amount from two bars preserves the difference between their tops. A ratio uses the whole readings. On an unfamiliar chart, write the baseline and tick interval before trusting what your eye sees.
S141.bridge: Read the first number on the vertical axis. Then watch what changes when the chart reveals the rest of each bar.

S149.title: How far can the apex travel?
transcript: Imagine sliding the top corner of a triangular sail sideways along a horizontal rail. The sail can look taller or more slanted. Can its area change while the base and the rail stay fixed?

The base is six centimetres long. The rail is four centimetres above it, measured at a right angle. Half of six times four is twelve. The sloping side grows as the peg travels, but the perpendicular height stays four, even beyond the end of the base.

A triangular field has a fence nine metres long along its base. A gate splits the fence into lengths four and five. Paths from the opposite corner divide the field into two triangles. The whole field is thirty six square metres. Find the area beside the longer fence.

Both triangles reach the same perpendicular height. Their areas are in the ratio four to five. Nine equal parts share thirty six square metres, so each part is four. The longer fence belongs to five parts, or twenty square metres.

A rectangle is twelve metres wide and eight metres high. Pick any point inside it and draw a line to each corner. The triangle along the bottom has an area of eighteen square metres. What is the area of the triangle along the top?

The top and bottom triangles each use a base of twelve. Their two perpendicular heights add to eight, however far sideways the point moves. Together their areas are half of twelve times eight, or forty eight square metres.

Subtract the bottom area of eighteen. The top area is thirty. To check, the bottom height must be three metres, since half of twelve times three is eighteen. The height left for the top is five, giving thirty again.

Mark the base and draw the height at a right angle, extending the base line when necessary. Triangles with a shared height divide area in the ratio of their bases. Equal parallel bases can be paired by adding their heights.
S149.bridge: Follow the perpendicular line from the moving corner to the base. Use that distance to compare the areas.

S150.title: What did the sun lamp reveal?

chapters.title: Two routes to a mixed pair

transcript: Five discs feel identical. Two show a sun and three show a moon. Mix them and draw without looking. Each disc is equally likely. Leave the first disc out when you draw the next one. How does that change your chances?
The first disc is a sun with probability two fifths. After that sun comes out, only one sun remains among four discs. The chance of two suns is two fifths times one quarter. That is one tenth.
Now try for one sun and one moon in either order. If a sun comes first, three of the four discs left are moons. If a moon comes first, how many of the four discs left are suns?

Two suns remain after a moon. Sun then moon has probability two fifths times three quarters. Moon then sun has probability three fifths times two quarters. Each order contributes six twentieths. They cannot happen together on one draw of two discs, so add them. Twelve twentieths simplifies to three fifths.

The machine now draws two discs in secret. A lamp lights exactly when at least one sun appears. You see the lamp light. What is the chance that both discs show suns? The lamp never tells you which disc came first.

Label the five discs so we can tell every ordered pair apart. Five choices for the first disc, then four for the second, make twenty equally likely pairs. The lamp stays dark only for two moons. Three choices followed by two give six dark pairs. Fourteen pairs are left when the lamp lights.

Only two of those fourteen pairs use both suns. Either sun can come first. Two out of fourteen is one seventh. Keep the remaining discs up to date on each draw. When a competition question gives you a clue, keep only the outcomes that could have produced it.
S150.bridge: When the lamp lights, find the pairs you can cross out before choosing the denominator.

S151.title: One socket, two plates

chapters.title: An account that will not balance

transcript: Imagine rebuilding a bridge deck out of rectangular plates. Each plate spans exactly two squares that share an edge. No gaps and no overlaps are allowed. Turning a plate changes its direction. What does it always keep?

Paint neighbouring squares in different colours. Put a dot on gold and a ring on blue. A horizontal plate covers one of each. Turn it upright. Still one of each. On this two by three deck, three upright plates give a complete covering.

The next deck is four squares by four. Leave the top left and bottom right corners open for inspection. Fourteen squares remain. Seven plates have the right area. Can seven plates actually cover this deck?

Before the openings, the deck had eight dots and eight rings. Both missing corners carried dots. Six dots and eight rings remain. Seven plates would need seven of each. One colour runs out early, whichever way you turn the plates.

Slide the lower opening up to the top right corner. This time one dot and one ring are missing. The counts balance. Can you prove that the plates fit? Cover the middle two squares of the top row. Put two horizontal plates in each row below. All seven fit.

Here is a different footbridge. Its rows hold three squares, one square, one square, then three squares. The narrow part runs down the middle. There are four dots and four rings. Is there room for four plates? Try to decide before any plate drops.

Look at the upper left tip. Its only neighbour is the top middle square. Covering that tip uses up the middle square. Now look at the upper right tip. It needs exactly the same neighbour. Two different plates cannot both use that square. The bridge cannot be covered, even though its colours balance.

Count the squares, then check the colours a single plate must cover. Unequal totals prove a covering impossible. When the counts balance, look for squares with just one neighbour. To prove that a covering exists, show a placement that fills every square exactly once.
S151.bridge: Follow the two ends of one plate. Watch what happens when both tips of the narrow deck need the same neighbour.

S152.title: The counter exchange
transcript: Two trays hold twenty counters altogether. Move three counters from the left tray to the right. The total stays twenty. Watch the gap: one side loses three at the same moment the other side gains three.
Start with twelve on the left and eight on the right. Move one across. The counts become eleven and nine. The difference shrinks from four to two. A single transfer changed the gap by two.
Two storage cases hold forty eight badges. After six badges move from the fuller case to the other, the cases contain equal numbers. How many badges were in each case before the move?

Equal shares of forty eight are twenty four each. Put the six badges back into the fuller case and remove them from the other. Thirty and eighteen are the original counts. Their difference is twelve, exactly twice the transfer.

Three trays contain thirty six counters. The first tray gives half its counters to the second. Then the second gives one third of its new pile to the third. All three finish equal. How many counters started in the first, second and third trays?

Finish with twelve in every tray. The second tray kept two thirds of its pile. Those two thirds are twelve, so each third is six. Just before that transfer the second tray held eighteen, and the third held only six. The first still held twelve.

The first tray kept half and ended with twelve. It must have started with twenty four and passed twelve to the second. Remove those twelve from eighteen. The starting counts were twenty four, six and six. Run both transfers forwards to check.

The words its new pile matter. A fraction acts on the contents at that moment. Mark the total, record who gives and receives, and run transfers backwards one at a time when the final amounts are known.
S152.bridge: When you undo a move, follow the same counters back to their original tray. Which pile was the fraction taken from?

S155.title: The palindrome odometer

chapters.title: Find the two kinds of gap

transcript: A four digit odometer reads three, four, four, three. It is a palindrome. Imagine putting a mirror between the middle wheels. Which wheels can you choose freely, and which are already determined?

The first two wheels show thirty four. Reflect them in reverse order to make thirty four, forty three. Advancing the first pair to thirty five produces three, five, five, three. The palindromes are a hundred and ten apart.
Now the odometer shows three, nine, nine, three. Predict the next palindrome. Be careful when the nine rolls back to zero.

The next possible first pair is forty. Its reflection is zero four, so the new reading is four thousand and four. Subtract three thousand nine hundred and ninety three. This time the gap is just eleven.

From one thousand and one through nine thousand nine hundred and ninety nine, how many whole numbers lie exactly halfway between two consecutive four digit palindromes? Count the gaps, without listing every address.

Hold the thousands wheel fixed. The hundreds wheel runs from zero to nine. Ten palindromes make nine gaps of one hundred and ten. Each even gap has one whole number exactly in its middle. There are nine possible nonzero thousands digits.

Nine groups of nine give eighty one halfway addresses. The eight carries between the groups each make a gap of eleven. Half of eleven is not a whole number, so those carries contribute none. Eighty one large gaps and eight small ones give eighty nine gaps among ninety palindromes.

A mirror makes the last two digits follow the first two. To find the next palindrome, increase the first pair and reflect it again. When counting a pattern, test the change at a carry before assuming every step is equal.
S155.bridge: Predict the display after 3993. Watch the gap on the number line when the hundreds wheel carries.

S009.title: The carry counter

chapters.title: Where did the zero come from?
The hundreds drawer can hold only one
The first tray that fills a hundred

transcript: Six loose counters arrive at two trays marked with the same letter. Split them equally. Three on this tray and three on its twin. A digit written twice must describe the same quantity both times.

Now each tray holds a two digit number ending in five. Together their total begins with seven. Tip the two groups of five into the units drawer. All ten fit in a sleeve worth one ten. The units drawer is empty. Its digit is zero.

The tens drawer shows seven sleeves. One just came across from the units. Take that one aside. Six sleeves remain, shared equally by the two trays. Each tray supplied three tens. Thirty five and thirty five make seventy.

Turn the counter round. Two copies of the number A B have made a three digit total labelled B C D. Different letters must have different digits. We want the smallest possible A B. Before opening the drawers, which letter can you name?

Even ninety nine doubled is only one hundred and ninety eight. The hundreds drawer must hold exactly one, so B is one. Move that digit back to both units places. One plus one leaves two units and sends nothing into the tens. D is two.

Four tens on each tray would make only eight tens. Five on each tray make ten tens. Exchange them for one hundred. No tens remain, so C is zero. Read the finished drawers: fifty one plus fifty one equals one hundred and two. Five, one, zero and two are all different. No smaller tens digit can work.

Now double sixty eight. Eight and eight make sixteen. Leave six in the units drawer and send one ten across. Six tens and six tens plus the carried ten make thirteen tens. Exchange ten of those tens for a hundred. The drawers read one hundred and thirty six. In a letter sum, keep the digit you write separate from the amount you carry.
S009.bridge: Track the sleeve that crosses from the units drawer into the tens drawer. Later, read the hundreds drawer first.

S010.title: The reversal line

chapters.title: Issue a ticket from two new clues

transcript: A ticket printer puts the same digit in two boxes. Together those digits add to eight, so each box shows four. Turning that ticket would change nothing. What changes when a ticket carries two different digits?

Slide the larger digit from units to tens. Each extra unit of digit difference now gains ten in one place and loses one in the other. The net gain is nine. A reversal that gains thirty six therefore moves a digit four larger into the tens place.

Our two digits also add to eight. Set four counters aside for the difference. The four left split into two matching pairs. The smaller digit is two and the larger is six. Print twenty six, then reverse it. Sixty two minus twenty six is thirty six.

Inspect a different pair of tickets. A B plus A C ends in zero, with hundreds digit B and tens digit D. All four letters use different digits. Find the smallest A B. Two two digit numbers cannot reach two hundred, so the new hundreds digit is one. B is one.

One plus C must end in zero. Only nine can complete the ten. Carry one. The tens total is twice A plus one. Four would give only nine, so the first candidate is five. Fifty one plus fifty nine equals one hundred and ten. Look at the hundreds and tens. Two different letters would both be one. Reject that ticket.

Move up one tens digit to six. Sixty one plus sixty nine makes one hundred and thirty. Read the four letters in order: six, one, nine, three. None collides. We have checked the only smaller candidate that could reach a hundred. The smallest legal first ticket is sixty one.

A fresh ticket gains twenty seven when you reverse its digits. The digits add to eleven. What is the ticket? Divide the gain by nine. The digits differ by three. Set three aside from eleven, then halve the eight left. The smaller digit is four, the larger seven. Check the journey: seventy four minus forty seven equals twenty seven. The ticket gaining value starts with the smaller digit.
S010.bridge: Follow the two digits when the ticket turns. At inspection, compare both the printed sum and the letters that received its digits.

S012.title: The missing rung
transcript: A beetle can climb one rung or two rungs in a jump. It starts on the ground. To reach rung two, it can jump straight there, or visit rung one first. Draw both routes with your finger.

How many routes reach rung three? Look backwards. The last jump came from rung two or rung one. Each route to rung two has one way to finish with a short jump. The single route to rung one can finish with a long jump. That makes three.
Now the third rung breaks. The beetle may fly over the gap, but it cannot land there. Does rung four become unreachable? Find the last safe place the beetle could have landed.

To land on four, the beetle must come from two. A jump from three is impossible. Both routes to two can cross the gap. Trace their different beginnings and their identical last jump. Write two routes beside four.

At every safe rung, add the counts at the two previous positions. Beside rung five write two. At six the counts are two and two, giving four. At seven they give six. At eight, six plus four gives ten. The zero stays in the log, holding the place of the broken rung.

A brass bell hangs on rung five. This time the beetle must land on that rung and ring the bell on its way to eight. Which of the ten routes count now? Imagine cutting a successful route into two pieces at the bell.

Two routes arrive at the bell. From five to eight the remaining climb is three rungs. The jumps can be three singles, a single followed by a double, or a double followed by a single. Each beginning accepts all three endings. Two groups of three give six bell routes.

Why did we add at a landing and multiply at the bell? Different final jumps put the routes in separate piles. At a compulsory stop, each beginning joins to each possible ending. Keep a zero for a forbidden landing. If a rule restricts the next jump, record how the route arrived as well.
S012.bridge: Pause when the film marks rung 3 as broken. Is rung 4 still reachable? Trace its possible final jumps before the film fills in the table.

S020.title: Clock turns and last digits

chapters.title: Five hours beyond a full turn

transcript: A cycle brings the same states back in the same order. Track where a full cycle ends and how many extra steps you take. When all you need is a last digit, you can multiply last digits and leave the rest of the number behind.

AMC Upper Primary practice can use a repeating picture, a clock or the last digit of a large power. Write a small first cycle. A Mawa style investigation can change the base or the number of steps. Check whether the cycle length stays the same.
It is nine o'clock on a twelve-hour clock. What number will the hour hand point to after seventeen hours? Start by removing any whole turns that bring you back to the same place.
Every twelve hours returns to the starting number. The seventeen hours leave five extra hours after full turns. Step five hours ahead. Wrap past twelve if needed, so the hour hand points to two.

What is the units digit of three to the power thirty-seven? Work with just the units digits of its first few powers. Watch for the first repeat. A remainder of zero will need a careful interpretation.

The first four units digits are three, nine, seven and one. The next digit repeats the first, and the same multiplication rule gives the same later digits. The exponent thirty-seven leaves a remainder of one on division by four. Use position one in the cycle. The digit at that position is three. If the remainder is zero, the fourth position sits at the end of the last full cycle.

Add the first fifty-one positive powers of three, starting with exponent one. What is the units digit of the sum? You already know the cycle of the last digits. Work out what one whole block contributes to the sum.

One full cycle has units digits three, nine, seven and one. Their sum is twenty, with units digit zero. There are twelve full cycles and three terms left. Every completed block contributes zero to the units digit. Add the first three digits of the cycle. Their sum is nineteen, so the final units digit is nine.

The first forty-eight powers make twelve full blocks. The next exponent is forty-nine. Its last digit is back at position one in the cycle. The last three digits to add are three, nine, and seven. Their sum is nineteen, so the units digit is nine.

If the step count is a multiple of the cycle length, land on the last listed item when the cycle was numbered from one. For a sum, add the contributions of the earlier terms as well as the final term. Check the total contributed by each full cycle.

Record states in order. Find the first state you can recognise again, and count the length from one occurrence to the next. Divide by the cycle length and use the remainder. When the task asks for a sum, work out what the full cycles contribute.
S020.bridge: For the sum in the film, 12 complete blocks use exponents 1 to 48. The next exponent is 49: which position is that in the repeating pattern of last digits?

S102.title: Digit sums and counting digits in ranges
S102.bridge: Keep the hundreds digit fixed and swap tens and units: 153 becomes 135. Count the printed threes in each column separately.

chapters.title: Digit sums and counting digits in ranges
Use a digit sum to find a remainder
Use a digit sum to find a remainder
Count occurrences in a list of consecutive numbers
Count occurrences in a list of consecutive numbers
Count a digit while writing only multiples of nine
Count a digit while writing only multiples of nine

transcript: A digit has a value and a position. The digit sum forgets the positions, but a count of written digits must consider every position. Break a range count into the ones, tens and hundreds places, then add those separate counts.

The AMC can ask how often a digit is written. Work in complete blocks, then inspect the last incomplete block. In Mawa primary application practice, digit sum restrictions can be combined with range restrictions. Use place value to prove which cases count.

What remainder does three hundred and eighty-six leave after division by nine? Use its digits to find the remainder without long division. Ten and one hundred both leave remainder one when divided by nine.

One hundred, ten and one each contribute the same remainder as one. The digit sum is three plus eight plus six, which is seventeen. The remainder of that sum is eight, which is also the remainder of three hundred and eighty-six.
Write every whole number from one through two hundred and forty-seven. How many times do you write the digit three? Each occurrence counts separately. Track the ones, tens and hundreds separately.

In the ones place every complete block of ten contributes one occurrence, with a possible extra at the end. The ones total is twenty-five. In the tens place, each complete hundred contains one run of ten occurrences. Include any matching part of the last hundred. That gives thirty. In the hundreds place, only the block starting at three hundred could match. It contributes zero. Adding the three totals gives fifty-five written occurrences.

Write the multiples of nine from one hundred through five hundred and ninety-nine, including any endpoint that is a multiple. Count every written three. Split the appearances among the three places. A number can contribute in more than one place.

Fix the ones digit at three. For hundreds digits one through five, the tens digits are five, four, three, two and one. Now keep the hundreds digit fixed and swap the tens and units digits. One hundred and fifty-three becomes one hundred and thirty-five. The digit sum and hundreds range are unchanged. Swapping back recovers the original, so this pairs the two lists exactly. The ones and tens columns contribute five each. Three hundred and thirty-three contributes once to each column.

For the hundreds place, fix the hundreds digit instead. The hundred block starting at three hundred contributes eleven occurrences, one for every multiple of nine in that block. Add the three position counts. An occurrence in one position is different from an occurrence in another, even in the same number. The total is twenty-one.

If a number contains the requested digit twice, it contributes two occurrences. Compare counting numbers with counting written digits. Digits zero and nine both have remainder zero on division by nine. Include both when zero is permitted in the position.

Write whether you need a sum, a number of valid integers or a count of written occurrences. Record the exact range. Use place-value blocks or digit-sum restrictions to organise the work. Check an endpoint and a number with a repeated digit before totalling.

S015.title: Two stamps for the mail train

chapters.title: Read only what each stamp needs

transcript: Parcels for the mail train are strapped in bundles of four. Seventeen parcels make four full bundles and one loose parcel. How many more parcels would fill that last bundle? Three. The remainder tells us what is already there. The gap tells us what is missing.

A parcel label earns a square stamp if its number divides evenly by four. It earns a triangle stamp if the number divides evenly by three. The four labels are three hundred and twenty four, three hundred and forty four, three hundred and fifty four, and three hundred and eighty four. Which get both stamps?

For the square stamp, inspect the last two digits. A hundred is divisible by four, so the hundreds place cannot spoil the test. Twenty four, forty four and eighty four pass. Fifty four fails. For the triangle stamp, add the digits. The three survivors have sums nine, eleven and fifteen. Only the first and last labels get both stamps.

A crate contains between twenty three and fifty nine parcels, including both ends. Add one parcel. Now the crate can be packed exactly in fours, and it can also be packed exactly in sixes. How many different original loads could it have held?

Push the whole interval one place to the right. Twenty three becomes twenty four, and fifty nine becomes sixty. We now need numbers in this shifted interval that the groups of four and the groups of six both reach.

Mark the multiples of four above the line, and the multiples of six below. Both first meet at twelve after zero. The same arrangement repeats every twelve. In our shifted interval, the shared stops are twenty four, thirty six, forty eight and sixty.

Each shared stop describes the crate after adding a parcel. Take one away from each. The original loads are twenty three, thirty five, forty seven and fifty nine. Four possibilities. Check the last one. The extra parcel makes sixty, which packs as fifteen fours or ten sixes.

A tempting answer keeps sixty and loses twenty three. That mixes two different number lines. Move the end stops when you change the quantity. Test the new quantity, then undo the change. For a different remainder problem, first ask whether one small move can make both divisions exact.
S015.bridge: When the film adds 1 to make a number divisible by both 4 and 6, pause. Where must the two ends of the search interval move? After finding a common multiple, how will you get back to the original number?

S019.title: The domino colour test

chapters.title: Build or rule out a covering

transcript: A chessboard may look like a collection of little squares. Its colours can reveal something numbers alone cannot: whether a covering is impossible.

In AMC, you may need to spot an odd or even pattern. In a Rossmoyne style problem, explain why every allowed piece follows the same rule. A MAWA investigation might explore which boards can be tiled. Let us move from pairs to colouring.
Start with a three by three chessboard. The top-left square is blue and the colours alternate. Count each colour. Is the number of squares odd or even?
There are five blue squares and four gold squares, nine altogether. They cannot all be grouped into pairs: one square remains.

Take a full four by four board. In the top row, cross out the two squares farthest to the left. One is blue and one is gold. Can dominoes cover the rest? Each domino covers two squares sharing an edge.
Yes. Place one domino across the remaining two squares in the top row. Then place two horizontal dominoes across each of the three lower rows. That is seven dominoes, covering fourteen squares.

Here is a harder puzzle. A four by four board has its top-left and bottom-right corners removed. Each domino covers two squares sharing an edge. The challenge is to cover the remaining board with seven dominoes and no overlap. Is that possible?
Colour the full board like a chessboard. There are eight blue squares and eight gold squares. Each domino, horizontal or vertical, covers one of each colour.
The two removed corners are both blue. That leaves six blue and eight gold squares. Seven dominoes would need seven of each colour. Since only six blue squares remain, the covering is impossible.

It is a mistake to stop at fourteen squares. Fourteen is divisible by two, but the colours do not balance. And colour balance alone does not guarantee a covering: the squares must still join up legally.
In an exam, identify what every allowed piece does. Pick a colouring that reveals the pattern. Count the colours and write a clear reason, not just an answer.
S019.bridge: In the film’s first 4-by-4 example, the crosses mark the two leftmost squares in the top row. Which domino covers the two top squares that remain? What would you have to change if the middle two had been removed instead?

S017.title: A frame around two tiles
transcript: A framer slides two upright edges and two level edges along the grout of a tiled wall. Once those four edges are fixed, the rectangle is fixed. A corner is a meeting of grout lines. A tile is the square between the lines.

Start with two square tiles side by side. How many rectangles can the framer outline? The top and bottom edges have no choice. There are three upright lines. Choose any two of them. The three outlines are the left tile, the right tile, and the whole strip.

The wall now has four columns and three rows. Call the amber tile A. It lies in the second row and the second column. Count rectangles that contain A. Choose a left edge on its left or farther out. How many right edges can still hold it inside?

The left slider has two positions. The right has three. The top and bottom sliders each have two. Each left choice works with every right choice, and every height pair. Multiply the four counts. Twenty four rectangles contain A.

Now mark tile B in the top row and third column. We want rectangles containing A but leaving B outside. A frame can miss B in more than one direction. Counting all the ways to miss it separately might count one frame twice. Which frames could we subtract instead?

Keep both marked tiles. Slide a small box around them. Its left boundary is set by A, and its right boundary by B. The top is set by B, and the bottom by A. Every rectangle containing both tiles must contain this whole box.

For both tiles, the left edge has two positions and the right edge has two. There is one top edge and there are two bottom edges. That gives eight frames containing both tiles. Of the twenty four that contained A, remove those eight. Sixteen rectangles keep A and leave B out.

Check the frame around A alone. It qualifies. Check the frame around the whole wall. It contains B, so it must disappear in the subtraction. On a new grid, locate the extreme marked tiles first. Count boundary lines on each side, and multiply choices that can be made independently.
S017.bridge: In the film’s marked grid, first count rectangles containing cell A. To remove the unwanted ones, which four boundary choices guarantee a rectangle contains both A and B?
